Entries.Text: Show the Tools window: Search, Called By, Palette and Problems.
Add an empty event to the selected file, after the selected event.
A new, empty event in {0}. Nothing starts it until an Initialize Event (or the game, for event 0 and 50) calls it.
Copy the selected event under the next free ID after it, with all its instructions and parameters.
Renumber the selected event, and optionally the Initialize Event calls in the same file that start it.
This is a common file: other files can start this event too, and their calls aren't changed. Use Called By to find them.
Remove the selected event (Ctrl+Z brings it back). Calls to it are left as they are, and reported in the log.
EMEVD Editor: deleted event {0}, which {1} Initialize Event calls in this file still start.
A whole number from 0 to 4294967295 that no other event of the file uses.
Type a whole number from 0 to 4294967295.
Event {0} already exists in this file.
Initialize Event lines in this file that start the event by its ID. Calls whose ID comes from a parameter aren't counted.
Change the event ID in those calls too, in the same undo step.
Add the event and select it.
Files searched so far. Files not opened yet are read as the search reaches them.
Stop the search; what was found is kept.
EMEVD Editor: the search for {0} failed.
Click to go there (Backspace in the Script window comes back).

The Initialize Event calls that start the selected event. The game uses the calling file's own event first, then common_func's, then common's: a map event can only be started from its own file, a common event from any file.
The event whose callers are listed, and where they're looked for.
Event {0} in {1}: any file can start it, so every file is searched.
Searching every file reads the ones not opened yet, which takes a moment.
Search every event file for calls that start this event.
Each Initialize Event line that starts the event. Calls whose ID comes from a parameter aren't listed: the ID is only known when the event runs.

Find instructions holding a value in any argument (an event flag, entity ID, param row…), and/or a kind of instruction. The layouts don't say which arguments are flags or entities, so search the number to see where it's used.
A whole number, or hex starting with 0x. Leave it empty to list every use of the instruction below. Arguments a parameter sets are skipped: their stored value is a placeholder.
Also match f32 arguments equal to the number, e.g. 10 finds a 10.0 second wait.
Only this instruction: its key (e.g. 2003[66]) or part of its name. Leave it empty to search every instruction.
Where to search. Every file reads the ones not opened yet, in the background.
Select a file (or an event) to search in.
Enter in either box searches too.
Search with the value and instruction above.
Clear the boxes and the results.
Each matching line, with the argument that holds the value.

Ready-made event patterns with fill-in fields. Built-in templates are patterns FromSoftware copied between many events of this game; their fields are the values that differ between the copies. Save your own from a selection or a whole event.
Your project's templates, then the built-ins by category. The category comes from the instructions' names and is only a guide.
The selected template, and where it came from.
Open the event this template was taken from, to see it in context.
Take this template out of the list. Its file is moved into an .archive folder beside it, not deleted.
The values to fill in. Each is written into every line that uses it. They start at the source event's values.
This template has no fields: it goes in as it is.
Default {0}. Written to {1} argument(s), on template line(s) {2}.
Put every field back to the source event's value.
Add the template with the fields filled in: as lines after the selected block, or as a new event. Either is one undo step.
The ID of the event Insert as New Event makes. It starts at the next free ID after the selected event.

Add the template's lines after the bottom selected block (or at the top when the event header is selected), like a paste. Event parameters in the template come with its lines, so check they match this event's.
Add the template as a new event under the ID above, after the selected event. Something still has to start it: an Initialize Event, or the game's own constructor event.
Select an event to insert the template's lines into.
Keep lines of this event as a project template. Every argument that refers to something (an entity, flag, param row, text or map) becomes a field; arguments holding the same value are one field.
Select an event to save lines from.
The name in the list, and the file name under .smithbox/Project/EMEVD/Templates.
A project template named {0} already exists.
Save the selected lines, in file order, with the event parameters that write them.
Save every line of the selected event, with its rest behaviour and parameters.
EMEVD Editor: failed to read templates {0}.
EMEVD Editor: failed to save template {0}.
EMEVD Editor: failed to remove template {0}.

Replace a value in many instructions at once, such as an event flag or entity ID used across a map. Preview lists every change first; Apply makes them as one undo step. Skip counts, goto labels and values an event parameter writes are never changed.
No event files are loaded for this project.
The value to find, or a range of values. Whole numbers or 0x hex; -1 also finds 4294967295 in unsigned arguments. Float arguments are not changed.
The value to find. With an end value below, every value from this one to that one.
Leave empty to find the one value above. Set it to find a whole range, e.g. to move a block of flags with Add.
Narrow which arguments change, so a number used as a flag isn't changed where it's an entity or a time.
Only arguments that refer to this kind of thing (from the instruction layouts). Any changes every matching integer argument.
Only row IDs of this param. For an argument whose param depends on another one (an item ID and its item type), the param it refers to on that line.
Instruction (optional), e.g. 2003[66] or Set Event Flag
Only lines of this instruction: its key, or part of its name.
Also change the event ID an Initialize Event starts. Off by default: renumbering an event is done with Change Event ID, which updates the event itself too.
Set To writes the same value everywhere. Add shifts each value by an amount (negative to go down), keeping a range in order.
A whole number or 0x hex. A value that doesn't fit an argument's type is listed but not changed.
Where to change: the selected event, the selected file, or every event file. Files not opened yet are read for the preview.
Enter the new value, or the amount to add.
The end of the range is below its start.
Preview first, check the list, then apply.
List every change this would make. Nothing is changed yet.
Make the ticked changes, as one undo step (Ctrl+Z undoes all of them). Values edited since the preview are left alone. Save writes the changed files.
EMEVD Editor: mass edit changed {0} values in {1} files.
EMEVD Editor: {0} values were edited since the preview and were left alone. Preview again to include them.
Every planned change. Untick one to leave it out; click a line to go to it.
{0} values wouldn't fit their argument's type and won't be changed.
Untick every change, to then tick only the ones wanted.
The new value doesn't fit this argument's type, so it can't be changed.
Deletes the selected block. A C-block goes with everything inside it, and a goto's closing label goes with it when nothing else jumps there.
a skip on line {0} would need a count of {1}, more than its count argument holds

Puts a new skip or goto in front of the selected blocks, making them a C-block that runs only when it doesn't jump. A skip's count is set for you; a goto gets a new label after the blocks. The new instruction's other arguments start at their defaults, so set its condition next.
Select blocks next to each other, in one block.
EMEVD Editor: the selection can't be wrapped: its blocks aren't next to each other in one block, a goto or skip outside them jumps into them, or no label ID is free.
EMEVD Editor: {0} was not done, it would add: {1}.

Double-click an instruction to insert it after the bottom selected block, or drag it onto the Script window: before a block, onto a C-block's foot for the end of that block, or onto the event header for the top. Its arguments start at their defaults.
The instruction layouts for this game didn't load.
Select an event to insert into.
Every instruction the game's layouts know, by class. Filter by name or by key, e.g. 2003[66].

The checks over every event of the selected file, run again whenever it changes. Click a problem to go to it. Vanilla files have a few of these too (gotos to labels they never define, calls passing fewer arguments than the event reads), so they aren't always mistakes. Block edits that would add one to an existing line are refused.
How many problems the selected file has, by kind.
Every problem, by event and line. Filter by event ID or problem kind.
The skip count runs past the last line of the event.
No label with this number comes after the goto.
An event parameter points at an instruction index the event doesn't have.
An event parameter writes at a byte that isn't the start of an argument, or past the instruction's arguments.
No layout decodes this instruction's bytes.
The Initialize Event passes fewer argument bytes (passed/needed) than the event it starts reads with its parameters.

Show skips and gotos as C-blocks holding the lines they jump over, with Else parts, and conditions just above the flow that evaluates them. Turn off to see every line flat, with every jump as a bracket in the margin. The file is the same either way.
Show each argument's name before its value in the blocks. Turn off to fit more values on a line.
Collapse every C-block and switch of the selected event to its header.
Expand every C-block and switch of the selected event.
EMEVD Editor: failed to read the instruction layouts {0}.
EMEVD Editor: failed to list the event files.
EMEVD Editor: failed to read the event names in {0}. The events are shown without names.
EMEVD Editor: failed to write {0}. It still has unsaved changes.
Write every event file with unsaved changes into the project folder, compressed as the game's file is. Files you haven't edited are left alone.
EMEVD Editor: '{0}' isn't a number. Type a whole number, or hex starting with 0x.
EMEVD Editor: {0} doesn't fit this argument ({1} to {2}).
EMEVD Editor: '{0}' isn't whole bytes of hex.
No layout decodes this instruction, so its bytes are edited directly. The length stays the same.
EMEVD Editor: the instruction has {0} bytes of arguments; type exactly that many.
What happens to the event when the player rests: keep running, restart from the top, or end.
This instruction jumps: changing its skip count or label changes which lines run. The brackets update as you edit.
Which of the event's start arguments writes this value when the event starts. With none, the value stored in the file is used.
Adds a slot after the event's last one. Every Initialize Event that starts this event must then pass a value for it, or the game reads past the arguments it was given.

The project's .emevd files. common holds the events that run everywhere, common_func the shared events other files start with Initialize Common Event, and each map file the events of that map. A file is read when first selected.
No .emevd files were found in the event folder.
The project has its own copy of this file.
The selected file's events, by ID. Names come from the .emeld beside the file, which only DS1, DS1R, BB and The Duskbloods ship. Filter by ID or name.
The file could not be read.

The selected event as blocks, one per instruction.
Click a value to edit it or link it to an event parameter. Drag a block to move it (a C-block moves with its body), or right-click it to copy, paste, duplicate, move or delete; Alt+Up/Down moves it, Ctrl+Z undoes, and Ctrl+S saves.
Ctrl+click adds or removes a block from the selection, Shift+click or Shift+Up/Down selects a range, and Ctrl+A selects the whole event; block edits and drags then act on every selected block.
Blue hexagons are conditions, orange blocks control flow, red blocks end the event, purple blocks start other events, and the other colours are commands by class.
A skip or goto that wraps whole blocks is a C-block holding the lines it jumps over (they run only when it doesn't jump), with an Else part when the body ends by jumping past one. A jump to the end of an enclosing block is marked as an exit. A run of gotos to labels that don't nest is a switch: its other gotos, a Default part for when none jump, then one Case per label. Click a block's caret (or press Left/Right) to collapse or expand it. Conditions sit just above the wait, skip, end or goto that evaluates them, joined by a strip.
Jumps that don't nest keep a bracket on the left: skips orange, gotos blue, red when they run past the end of the event or miss their label.
Yellow pills are event parameters: the value comes from the arguments the event is started with.
Up/Down moves the selection, Enter or a double-click follows an Initialize Event, and Backspace goes back.
A switch's default part: what runs when none of its gotos jump. Drop a block here to add it at the start of the default part.

Block edits (move, copy, cut, duplicate, delete, drag) act on every selected line. A selected C-block takes its body with it, so lines inside it count once. The fields below are the line clicked last.
The end of this C-block. Drop a block here to add it at the end of the block.
Back to the event you jumped from (Backspace).
Instructions with no layout, or whose bytes fit none of its forms. They are shown as raw bytes. Vanilla files have none, so these come from mods or a layout gap.
Event parameters that point at no instruction, or at a byte that isn't the start of an argument. The game would write the value into the wrong place.

Skips that run past the end of the event, or gotos with no matching label after them. Shown as red brackets.
Vanilla files have some of these too (e.g. Elden Ring common event 715 jumps to label 1, which it never defines), so they aren't always mistakes; what the game does with them isn't confirmed.
The event header. Click to see its parameters in the Properties window.

{0}
No layout for this instruction: shown as raw bytes.
Double-click or press Enter to go to the event it starts.
The selected instruction's layout and arguments, or the event header's parameters when the header is selected.
Select an event or an instruction.
Each parameter copies bytes of the event's start arguments (slot X<offset>_<size>) over an argument of one instruction when the event starts.
Optional: some vanilla uses end before this argument.
Inferred: not in any shipped definition, worked out from the game's data.
Set by an event parameter when the event starts. The file holds {0} here.
Event {0} isn't in this file, common_func or common.
{0}, from {1}: Reference is DarkScript3's arg types in the imported reference EMEDFs; Shipped is the game's own Japanese arg name.
Param row (the param depends on a value no layout names)
Show entity {0} in the Map Editor (loads {1}).
This file isn't a map's, so the entity's map isn't known: search every event file for {0} instead.
Search every event file for event flag {0}.
Open {0} row {1} in the Param Editor.
Open {0} entry {1} in the Text Editor.
Another game's definition fits every vanilla use, and Bloodborne and The Duskbloods agree on it. Very likely right.
One other game's definition fits every vanilla use. The layout is proven by the data; the name is a suggestion, since the same ID can be a different instruction in another game.
The layout was built from how the game exe reads the arguments. It has no shipped name.
No definition fits: the layout was inferred from the vanilla data alone. It has no names.
